<DIV align="center">
<B>NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS</B>
</DIV>

<DIV align="center">
<B>(unaudited)</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<B>1.&nbsp; Financial Statements</B>&nbsp;&#151; The financial
data presented herein are unaudited, but in the opinion of
management reflect those adjustments necessary for a fair
presentation of such information. Results for interim periods
should not be considered indicative of results for a full year.
Reference should be made to the financial statements contained in
 the registrant&#146;s prospectus dated June&nbsp;13, 2000 as
filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on
June&nbsp;14, 2000. For purposes of Notes to Financial
Statements, &#147;Visteon&#148; or the &#147;Company&#148; means
Visteon Corporation and its majority owned subsidiaries unless
the context requires otherwise.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Visteon is the world&#146;s second largest supplier of automotive
 systems, modules and components to global vehicle manufacturers.
 Ford Motor Company (&#147;Ford&#148;) established Visteon as a
wholly-owned subsidiary in January&nbsp;2000, and subsequently
contributed or otherwise transferred to Visteon the assets and
liabilities comprising Ford&#146;s automotive components and
systems business. Visteon became an independent company when Ford
 distributed all of the shares (130&nbsp;million) of Visteon
common stock to the holders of record on June&nbsp;12, 2000 of
Ford common and Class&nbsp;B stock (the &#147;spin-off&#148;).

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Visteon recorded a pre-tax charge of approximately
$13&nbsp;million ($8 million after-tax) in the second quarter of
2000 for Visteon-designated employees that are part of special
voluntary retirement and separation programs announced previously
 by Visteon.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<B>3.&nbsp; Debt</B>&nbsp;&#151; During the second quarter of
2000, Visteon established a commercial paper program under which,
 at June&nbsp;30, 2000, about $410&nbsp;million was outstanding
with maturities ranging up to 35&nbsp;days and a weighted average
 interest rate of 6.9%. In addition, Visteon entered into
financing arrangements with third-party lenders to provide up to
a total of $2.0&nbsp;billion of contractually committed,
unsecured revolving credit facilities. The revolving credit
facilities are evenly split between 364-day and 5-year
commitments, maturing in June&nbsp;2001 and June&nbsp;2005,
respectively. Borrowings under the revolving credit facilities
bear interest based on a variable interest rate option selected
at the time of borrowing. No amounts were outstanding under the
revolving credit facilities at June&nbsp;30, 2000.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
In June&nbsp;2000, Visteon borrowed $1.2&nbsp;billion under a
short-term, unsecured financing arrangement with a third-party
lender. Obligations under this arrangement mature in
December&nbsp;2000. Interest is paid based on a variable interest
 rate option selected at the time of borrowing (approximately 7%
at June&nbsp;30, 2000). Based on management&#146;s intent and
capability to refinance this obligation through a long-term
financing arrangement, $1.0&nbsp;billion of this obligation has
been classified as long-term debt on the accompanying
June&nbsp;30, 2000 balance sheet.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<B>4.&nbsp; Pension and Other Postretirement Benefits</B>
&nbsp;&#151; Under the terms of Visteon&#146;s separation from
Ford, Ford has retained the pension, postretirement health care
and postretirement retiree life insurance obligations for most
Visteon-designated employees of Ford who retired prior to the
spin-off. Ford also retained the related Voluntary
Employees&#146; Beneficiary Association assets. The asset and
liability transfers between Ford and Visteon postretirement
benefit plans reduced Visteon&#146;s net postretirement related
liabilities by about $1.5&nbsp;billion to about $2&nbsp;billion
at June&nbsp;30, 2000. Demographic and actuarial assumptions were
 used in estimating liability transfers at separation.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<B>5.&nbsp; Income Per Share of Common Stock</B>&nbsp;&#151;
Basic income per share of Common Stock is calculated by dividing
the income attributable to Common Stock by the average number of
shares of Common Stock outstanding during the applicable period,
adjusted for restricted stock. For purposes of the earnings per
share calculations, 130&nbsp;million shares of common stock are
treated as outstanding for periods prior to our spin-off from
Ford. The calculation of diluted income per share of Common Stock
 takes into account the effect of dilutive potential common
stock, such as stock options and other stock-based awards.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Visteon sponsors a stock-based incentive plan (&#147;Long-Term
Incentive Compensation Plan&#148; or &#147;LTIP&#148;). Effective
 at the date of the spin-off, Visteon granted to employees about
800,000 shares of restricted stock and about 2&nbsp;million stock
 options with an exercise price equal to the average of the
highest and lowest prices at which Visteon common stock was
traded on the New York Stock Exchange on that date. The
restricted stock will vest on the fifth anniversary of the date
of grant. Such stock is considered compensation for services to
be provided by employees and the related expense will be
recognized over the term of the services provided. Stock options
will become exercisable 33% after one year from the date of
grant, an additional 33% after two years and in full after three
years, and expire after 10&nbsp;years from the date of grant.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Net transfers and settlements of balances are primarily related
to Ford converting $1,120&nbsp;million of debt owed to it by
Visteon under an intracompany revolving loan arrangement into an
equity investment in Visteon, Ford retaining about
$573&nbsp;million of prepaid health care amounts related to
active employees, and asset and liability transfers between Ford
and Visteon postretirement benefit plans, net of related deferred
 taxes.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<B>10.&nbsp; Other</B>&nbsp;&#151; On July&nbsp;13, 2000, the
Board of Directors of Visteon declared a quarterly dividend of
$0.06&nbsp;per share on the Company&#146;s common stock. The
dividend is payable on September&nbsp;1, 2000 to shareholders of
record as of August&nbsp;2, 2000.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
On June&nbsp;2, 2000, Visteon and Ford signed a non-binding
letter of intent with Pilkington plc, relating to Visteon&#146;s
Glass business. The parties have agreed to negotiate the terms of
 a joint venture, to be owned 80.1% by Pilkington and 19.9% by
Visteon, which would acquire Visteon&#146;s Glass business for
cash consideration and assumption of certain liabilities and
would assume operational management of that business.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
For the year ended December&nbsp;31, 1999, the Glass segment
represented about 6% of Visteon&#146;s average assets, 4% of
Visteon&#146;s total sales and less than one half of one percent
of Visteon&#146;s net income. Visteon&#146;s Carlite&#174;
aftermarket operations would be included in the business to be
transferred

to the joint venture. In connection with the transaction, Ford
would enter into a separate supply agreement with the joint
venture, which would supersede Ford&#146;s supply agreement with
Visteon as it relates to the Glass segment. If a definitive
agreement is reached, we expect to complete this transaction
during 2000. If completed, and dependent upon the terms
ultimately agreed to, this transaction would likely result in
Visteon incurring a significant charge to earnings. The letter of
 intent is non-binding, however, there is no assurance that a
definitive agreement will be reached, or that it will not differ
materially from the description above.

<P align="center"><B>REPORT OF INDEPENDENT ACCOUNTANTS</B>

<P align="left">To the Board of Directors and Stockholders

<DIV align="left">
Visteon Corporation
</DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
We have reviewed the accompanying consolidated balance sheet of
Visteon Corporation and Subsidiaries as of June&nbsp;30, 2000,
and the related consolidated statement of income for the
three-month and six-month periods ended June&nbsp;30, 2000, and
the condensed consolidated statement of cash flows for the
six-month period ended June&nbsp;30, 2000. These financial
statements are the responsibility of the Company&#146;s
management.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
We conducted our review in accordance with standards established
by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants. A
review of interim financial information consists principally of
applying analytical procedures to financial data and making
inquiries of persons responsible for financial and accounting
matters. It is substantially less in scope than an audit
conducted in accordance with generally accepted auditing
standards, the objective of which is the expression of an opinion
 regarding the financial statements taken as a whole.
Accordingly, we do not express such an opinion.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Based on our review, we are not aware of any material
modifications that should be made to the accompanying
consolidated interim financial statements for them to be in
conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the
United States.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
We have previously audited in accordance with auditing standards
generally accepted in the United States, the consolidated balance
 sheet as of December&nbsp;31, 1999, and the related consolidated
 statements of income, stockholders&#146; equity, and cash flows
for the year then ended (not presented herein); and in our report
 dated April&nbsp;7, 2000, except as to Note&nbsp;1 for which the
 date was June&nbsp;1, 2000, we expressed an unqualified opinion
on those consolidated financial statements. In our opinion, the
information set forth in the accompanying consolidated balance
sheet as of December&nbsp;31, 1999, is fairly stated, in all
material respects, in relation to the consolidated balance sheet
from which it has been derived.

<P align="left">
/s/&nbsp; PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP

<P align="left">
July&nbsp;17, 2000

<P align="left"><B>Overview</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Ford Motor Company established Visteon Corporation as a
wholly-owned subsidiary in January&nbsp;2000 and subsequently
contributed or otherwise transferred to Visteon the assets and
liabilities comprising Ford&#146;s automotive components and
systems business. On June&nbsp;28, 2000 Ford completed its
spin-off of Visteon by distributing shares of Visteon common
stock on a pro rata basis to the holders of Ford common and
Class&nbsp;B stock. Visteon is the world&#146;s second largest
supplier of automotive systems, modules and components to global
vehicle manufacturers.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Our worldwide sales were $5.3&nbsp;billion in the second quarter
of 2000, compared with $5.1&nbsp;billion actual and
$4.9&nbsp;billion pro forma in the second quarter of 1999. The
increase compared with 1999 reflects primarily sales gained from
the consolidations of Halla Climate Control and Duck Yang (we
increased our ownership interest from 35% to 70% in Halla Climate
 Control, and purchased 51% ownership interest in Duck Yang); the
 acquisitions of the automotive interiors division of Compagnie
Plastic Omnium and Naldec; and higher sales volume for trucks,
primarily in North America. Year-over-year price reductions,
including a one-time price realignment of 5% that resulted from a
 joint Ford-Visteon competitive pricing study, are a partial
offset.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Worldwide net income was $162&nbsp;million in the second quarter
of 2000, compared with $280&nbsp;million actual and
$170&nbsp;million pro forma in the second quarter of 1999. The
reduction in net income compared with 1999 actual results was
more than accounted for by the one-time price realignment, with
Ford, of 5%. This year&#146;s results also include a charge of
$8&nbsp;million for employees that are part of special voluntary
retirement and separation programs in Europe, and the previously
announced closure of the Dearborn Glass Plant.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Worldwide sales totaled $10.5&nbsp;billion in the first half of
2000, compared with $9.8&nbsp;billion actual and
$9.5&nbsp;billion pro forma in the first half of 1999. The
increase in sales reflects primarily higher volume, primarily in
North America, the consolidations of Halla Climate Control and
Duck Yang, and the acquisitions of the automotive interiors
division of Compagnie Plastic Omnium and Naldec. The
year-over-year price reductions, previously referred to, are a
partial offset.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Our worldwide net income was $309&nbsp;million in the first half
of 2000, compared with $485&nbsp;million actual and
$252&nbsp;million pro forma in 1999. The decrease in net income
compared with 1999 actual earnings was more than accounted for by
 the one-time price realignment with Ford, of 5&nbsp;percent,
referred to above. Continued strong sales volume and cost
reductions were a partial offset to price reductions.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Unaudited pro forma consolidated financial data for 1999 has been
 derived from the application of pro forma adjustments to our
consolidated financial statements and give effect to our spin-off
 from Ford. The pro forma financial data has been prepared as if
the spin-off from Ford had occurred

	$9.5&nbsp;billion, had the one-time 5% price reduction effective

	 would have decreased by about $33 million, as a result of added
	incremental corporate costs, insurance and risk management costs
	incurred as a result of operating Visteon as a stand-alone
	company and for a reduction to profit sharing expense. This
	profit-sharing adjustment reflects our agreement with Ford that
	Visteon&#146;s liability, for profit sharing payments based on
	Ford&#146;s profits made to Ford workers that are assigned to us,
	 will be limited to $50&nbsp;million per year through 2004.</TD>

	$45&nbsp;million to $70 million as a result of reductions in

Sales in the second quarter of 2000 totaled $5.3&nbsp;billion
compared with $5.1&nbsp;billion in the second quarter of 1999, an
 increase of $246&nbsp;million or 4.9%. Sales for our Comfort,
Communication &#38; Safety

<!-- PAGEBREAK -->

in the second quarter of 1999, an increase of $245&nbsp;million
or 10.2%. Sales for our Dynamics &#38; Energy Conversion segment
were $2.5&nbsp;billion, a decrease of $1&nbsp;million from the
second quarter of 1999. Glass sales were $204&nbsp;million in the
 second quarter of 2000, compared with $202&nbsp;million in the
second quarter of 1999, an increase of $2&nbsp;million. The
increase in sales for our Comfort, Communication &#38; Safety
segment was more than accounted for by the consolidations of
Halla Climate Control and Duck Yang (we increased our ownership
interest from 35% to 70% in Halla Climate Control, and purchased
51% ownership interest in Duck Yang), and the acquisition of the
automotive interiors division of Compagnie Plastic Omnium. Sales
for our Comfort, Communications and Safety segment also increased
 as a result of higher sales volume to Ford and our other
customers; price reductions granted to Ford and our other
customers were a partial offset. Sales for our Dynamics and
Energy Conversion segment reflect primarily higher sales volume
to Ford and our other customers. Sales for our Dynamics and
Energy Conversion segment also increased reflecting the
acquisition of Naldec. These increases were offset by price
reductions granted to Ford and our other customers. Total sales
from consolidations and acquisitions increased second quarter
sales by about $380&nbsp;million. The increase in sales for our
Glass segment reflects higher sales volume, and to a lesser
extent customer product content changes, offset largely by price
reductions granted to Ford and our other customers.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Net income for our Comfort, Communication &#38; Safety segment
was $141 million in the second quarter of 2000, down
$41&nbsp;million from the second quarter of 1999. The reduction
was primarily a result of price reductions, offset partially by
higher sales volume and lower costs. Net income for our Dynamics
&#38; Energy Conversion segment was $42&nbsp;million in the
second quarter of 2000, a decrease of $64&nbsp;million. This
decrease reflected primarily price reductions and, to a lesser
extent, premiums associated with continued higher operating
volumes and employee separation costs for a voluntary retirement
program in Europe, offset partially by lower costs. Net loss for
Glass was $15&nbsp;million compared with net income of
$8&nbsp;million in the second quarter of 1999, a decline of
$23&nbsp;million. The decrease reflected costs associated with
the previously announced closure of the Dearborn Glass Plant and
price reductions.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Sales in the first half of 2000 totaled $10.5&nbsp;billion
compared with $9.8 billion in the first half of 1999, an increase
 of $699&nbsp;million or 7.1%. Sales for our Comfort,
Communication &#38; Safety segment were $5.3&nbsp;billion,
compared with $4.6&nbsp;billion in the first half of 1999, an
increase of $645&nbsp;million or 14.0%. Sales for our Dynamics
&#38; Energy Conversion segment were $4.9&nbsp;billion, up
$55&nbsp;million or 1.1% from the first half of 1999. Glass sales
 were $401 million in the first half of 2000, compared with
$402&nbsp;million in the first half of 1999, a decrease of
$1&nbsp;million. Sales for our Comfort, Communication &#38;
Safety segment increased due to the consolidations of Halla
Climate Control and Duck Yang and the acquisition of the
automotive interiors division of Compagnie Plastic Omnium. Sales
for our Comfort, Communication &#38; Safety segment also
increased as a result of higher sales volumes to Ford and our
other customers. The increase in sales for our Dynamics and
Energy Conversion segment reflects primarily higher sales volume
to Ford and our other customers and the acquisition of Naldec.
Total sales from consolidations and acquisitions increased first
half sales by about $640&nbsp;million. The increases for both
segments were offset partially by price reductions granted to
Ford and our other customers. The decrease in sales for our Glass
 segment reflects price reductions granted to Ford and our other
customers, offset by higher sales volume, and to a lesser extent
customer product content changes.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Net income for our Comfort, Communication &#38; Safety segment
was $255 million in the first half of 2000, down $48&nbsp;million
 from the first half of 1999. The reduction was primarily a
result of price reductions, offset partially by higher sales
volume and lower costs. Net income for our Dynamics &#38; Energy
Conversion segment was $92&nbsp;million in the first half of
2000, a decrease of $93&nbsp;million. This decrease was primarily
 a result of price reductions and premiums associated with
continued higher operating volumes; partially offset by higher
sales volume, and lower costs. Net loss for Glass was $(19)
million as compared with net income of $13&nbsp;million in the
first half of 1999, a decline of

<P align="left"><B>Liquidity and Capital Resources</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Our historical balance sheet reflects cash and cash equivalents
of $965 million and short-term and long-term debt of
$2.1&nbsp;billion at June&nbsp;30, 2000 and cash and cash
equivalents of $1.8&nbsp;billion and short-term and long-term
debt of $2.3&nbsp;billion at December&nbsp;31, 1999. All
short-term and long-term debt at June&nbsp;30, 2000 was owed to
third parties. The short-term and long-term debt at
December&nbsp;31, 1999 consisted of $1.1&nbsp;billion owed to
Ford under an intracompany revolving loan agreement, about
$800&nbsp;million owed by Visteon subsidiaries to Ford
subsidiaries, and the remainder was owed to third parties.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Our debt exceeded our cash and cash equivalents by
$1.1&nbsp;billion at June&nbsp;30, 2000 and by $470&nbsp;million
at December&nbsp;31, 1999. Our ratio of total debt to total
capital, which consists of total debt plus equity, was 37% at
June&nbsp;30, 2000 and 61% at December&nbsp;31, 1999.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
During the second quarter of 2000, we entered into various
financing arrangements totaling $5.2&nbsp;billion in available
credit. We entered into financing agreements with third-party
lenders to provide up to a total of $2.0&nbsp;billion of
contractually committed, unsecured revolving credit facilities.
These facilities are evenly split between 364-day and 5-year
commitments, maturing in June, 2001 and June, 2005, respectively.
 As of June 30, 2000 we had no borrowings under these global
credit facilities. In the second quarter we also entered into a
short-term, unsecured credit agreement with a lender providing up
 to $1.2&nbsp;billion for general corporate purposes. As of
June&nbsp;30, 2000, we had borrowed all $1.2&nbsp;billion
available under this facility. This short-term facility matures
in December&nbsp;2000 and is expected to be repaid in full with
the proceeds from long-term financing and other available funds.
We also have entered into a commercial paper program providing up
 to $2.0&nbsp;billion of borrowing ability. As of June&nbsp;30,
2000, the outstanding balance under our commercial paper program
was $410&nbsp;million with maturities ranging up to 35&nbsp;days
and a weighted average interest rate of 6.9%, we intend not to
exceed $3.2&nbsp;billion of borrowing under these facilities as
we view the unsecured revolving credit facilities and the
commercial paper program as substitutes for one another.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
We expect cash flow from operations and borrowings to satisfy
future working capital, capital expenditures, research and
development, pension funding, dividend and debt service
requirements for at least the next year.

<P align="left"><B>Cash Flows</B>

<P align="left"><I>Operating Activities</I>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Cash flows used in operating activities during the first six
months of 2000 totaled about $1.6&nbsp;billion, compared with
cash flows provided by operating activities of about
$1.2&nbsp;billion for the same period in 1999. The decrease in
2000 was caused primarily by changes in receivables, payables and
 other working capital items resulting primarily from effects
associated with our spin-off from Ford, including payments
totaling about $570&nbsp;million to Ford to prepay certain
healthcare costs for active employees.

<P align="left"><I>Investing Activities</I>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Cash used in investing activities was $297&nbsp;million during
the first six months of 2000 compared with $927&nbsp;million for
the same period in 1999. During the first half of 1999, we
acquired the automotive interiors division of Compagnie Plastic
Omnium, headquartered in France, for about

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Our capital expenditures were $284&nbsp;million during the first
six months of 2000, compared to $384&nbsp;million for the same
period in 1999. The decrease in capital spending in 2000 reflects
 timing of product programs, investment projects and equipment
receipts. We currently expect about $930&nbsp;million in capital
expenditures in 2000.

<P align="left"><I>Financing Activities</I>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Cash provided by financing activities totaled $1.0&nbsp;billion
in the first six months of 2000 compared with $725&nbsp;million
in the first six months of 1999. For the first half of 2000, cash
 provided by financing activities reflects proceeds from
issuances of commercial paper and borrowings under a
$1.2&nbsp;billion short-term unsecured financing arrangement with
 a third-party lender, net of payments of debt primarily from
Ford. For the first half of 1999, cash provided by financing
activities reflects additional debt associated with acquisition
activities. Our cash balance will be reduced by $100&nbsp;million
 after June&nbsp;30, 2000 for a scheduled payment to Ford as part
 of our separation arrangements.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
On July&nbsp;13, 2000, the Visteon Board of Directors declared a
quarterly dividend on Visteon common stock of $0.06 per share,
payable on September&nbsp;1, 2000 to holders of record on
August&nbsp;2, 2000.

<P align="left"><B>Strategic Initiatives</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Through the course of the second quarter we initiated a number of
 actions that will further improve our business prospects. First
was the announcement of a Letter of Intent outlining terms of a
joint venture regarding our Glass business. On June&nbsp;2, 2000,
 Visteon and Ford signed a non-binding letter of intent with
Pilkington plc, relating to Visteon&#146;s Glass business. The
parties have agreed to negotiate the terms of a joint venture, to
 be owned 80.1% by Pilkington and 19.9% by Visteon, which would
acquire Visteon&#146;s Glass business for cash consideration and
assumption of certain liabilities and would assume operational
management of that business. We are targeting to complete the
transaction by the end of 2000. Secondly, to strengthen our
telematics business, we have agreed to establish a joint venture
with Lernout and Hauspie to enable us to further strengthen our
position as a leader in automotive voice technologies, we formed
an affiliation with Samsung Electronics, Co., Ltd. to develop
fully integrated high-quality telematics products, and we
established a relationship with Sirius Satellite Radio to combine
 Visteon&#146;s multimedia expertise with Sirius&#146;
100-channel audio entertainment service. A third action planned
is an investment in a new A/C compressor plant in Eastern Europe
to provide a fuel-efficient air conditioning system to meet the
growing demand in Europe. A fourth action planned is the
agreement to work with PSA Peugeot-Citro&#235;n to develop a next
 generation climate control system. This will allow us to develop
 a system aimed at improving passenger comfort and optimizing
in-vehicle global thermal system management.

<P align="left"><B>Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
We are exposed to a variety of market risks, including foreign
currency exchange rates, interest rates and commodity prices,
which could impact our financial results. The effect of changes
in exchange rates, interest rates and commodity prices on our
earnings generally have been small relative to other factors that
 also affect earnings, such as unit sales and operating margins.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
We use derivative financial instruments as part of an overall
risk management program in order to reduce the potentially
adverse impact from these financial risks. Derivative instruments
 are not used for speculative purposes, as per clearly defined
risk management policies.

<P align="left"><I>Foreign Currency Risk</I>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Our net cash inflows and outflows exposed to the risk of changes
in exchange rates arise from the sale of products in countries
other than the manufacturing source, foreign currency denominated
 supplier payments, debt and other payables, subsidiary dividends
 and investments in subsidiaries. Our ongoing solution is to
reduce the exposure through operating actions. In the near-term,
we use foreign exchange forward contracts to manage our exposure.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Our primary foreign exchange exposure includes the euro,
Brazilian Real, Mexican Peso and the Canadian Dollar. Because of
the mix between our costs and revenues in various regions, we are
 generally exposed to weakening of the euro and to strengthening
of the Brazilian Real, Mexican Peso and Canadian Dollar. For
transactions in these currencies, we utilize a strategy of
partial coverage. As of June&nbsp;30, 2000, our coverage for
projected transactions in these currencies for the remainder of
2000 ranged from 0% to about 70%. As of June&nbsp;30, 2000, a 10%
 adverse change in exchange rates from prevailing rates for all
of these currencies would result in an adverse impact on net
income of about $25&nbsp;million on an annual basis.

<P align="left"><I>Interest Rate Risk</I>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
At June&nbsp;30, 2000 most of our borrowings were on a variable
rate basis. As discussed in Note&nbsp;3, of Notes to Financial
Statements, we intend to refinance an obligation under a
short-term, unsecured financing arrangement with a third party
lender through a long-term financing arrangement. This long-term
financing arrangement is likely to bear interest at a fixed rate,
 reducing Visteon&#146;s exposure to changes in interest rates.

<P align="left"><I>Commodity Risk</I>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
We have entered into fixed price contracts with some of our key
suppliers to protect us from changes in market prices for the
non-ferrous metals used in the manufacturing of automotive
components. As a result, we have no need presently to enter into
financial derivatives to hedge these potential exposures. The
risk to these exposures may be managed with the use of financial
derivatives if in the future we enter into floating price
contracts with our key suppliers.

<P align="left"><B>New Accounting Standards</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Statement of Financial Accounting Standards No.&nbsp;133
(&#147;SFAS&nbsp;133&#148;), &#147;Accounting for Derivative
Instruments and Hedging Activities,&#148; was issued by the
Financial Accounting Standards Board in June&nbsp;1998.
SFAS&nbsp;133 provides a comprehensive and consistent standard
for the recognition and measurement of derivatives and hedging
activities. We have not adopted SFAS&nbsp;133 based on the
May&nbsp;1999 announcement by the Financial Accounting Standards
Board to delay by one year the implementation date of
SFAS&nbsp;133 until January&nbsp;1, 2001. We have not yet
determined the effect of adopting SFAS 133.

<P align="left"><B>Other Financial Information</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP, our independent public accountants,
performed a limited review of the financial data presented on
pages&nbsp;1 through 8 inclusive. The review was performed in
accordance with standards for such reviews established by the
American Institute of Certified Public Accountants. The review
did not constitute an audit; accordingly, PricewaterhouseCoopers
LLP did not express an opinion on the aforementioned data. Their
review report included herein is not a &#147;report&#148; within
the meaning of Sections&nbsp;7 and 11 of the 1933 Act and the
independent accountant&#146;s liability under Section&nbsp;11
does not extend to it. The financial data includes any material
adjustments or disclosures proposed by PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP
 as a result of their review.

<P align="left"><B>ITEM&nbsp;1.&nbsp; LEGAL PROCEEDINGS</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
We are involved in routine litigation incidental to the conduct
of our business. We do not believe that any litigation to which
we are currently a party will have a material adverse effect on
our financial condition.

<P align="left"><B>ITEM&nbsp;2.&nbsp; CHANGES IN SECURITIES AND USE OF PROCEEDS
</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
On June&nbsp;28, 2000, Ford completed its spin-off of Visteon by
distributing shares of Visteon common stock on a pro rata basis
to the holders of Ford common and Class&nbsp;B stock. This
offering was effected pursuant to a Registration Statement on
Form&nbsp;S-1 of the Registrant (Registration
No.&nbsp;333-38388), declared effective by the SEC on
June&nbsp;7, 2000. The offering commenced on the effective date
of the Registration Statement and terminated with the
distribution of all of the securities that had been registered,
consisting of 130&nbsp;million shares of the Registrant&#146;s
common stock. Since this was not an offering for cash, there were
 no proceeds from the spin-off. The total expenses incurred by
the Registrant relative to issuance and distribution of its
common stock from the effective date of the Registration
Statement through June&nbsp;30, 2000 are estimated at $750,000.
Of this amount, no amount consisted of direct or indirect
payments to directors or officers of Visteon or their associates,
 to Ford, or to other affiliates of Visteon, and $750,000
consisted of direct or indirect payments to others.
